title: Prefix and Suffix Search
description: Brute force to optimized: scanning every word directly per query versus a combined suffix-separator-word trie.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Problem Summary: Design a WordFilter initialized with a list of words, supporting f(prefix, suffix), which returns the largest index of a word in the list that has BOTH the given prefix AND the given suffix; return -1 if no such word exists.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Match BOTH a prefix and a suffix simultaneously\"","Neither condition alone maps to a single trie; combining suffix and word into one search key with a separator turns this into ONE prefix search"],["\"Return the LARGEST matching index\"","Storing (and overwriting with) the max index seen at every trie node as words are inserted in order answers this directly"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

A trie naturally answers prefix questions, not suffix-plus-prefix questions. The key trick is inserting, for every word, EVERY combination of "some suffix of the word" concatenated with a separator character and then the FULL word, for each possible suffix. A query for f(prefix, suffix) becomes searching for suffix concatenated with the separator and then prefix, as a PREFIX of one of these inserted combo strings.

blocks.title: Analogy: A Card Catalog Indexed Both by Ending and Beginning
blocks.text: Picture a card catalog where every book is filed multiple times: once for each way of describing it by "this ending, then the full title". Looking up "starts with X and ends with Y" becomes one single lookup of "Y then X" in this specially organized catalog.

blocks.caption: Insert suffix + separator + full word, for every suffix of every word, into one trie

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: words = ["apple"], f("a", "e")
Result: 0. "apple" starts with "a" and ends with "e", the only word, index 0.
Example: words = ["apple", "apply", "app"]
f("app","y")=1 ("apply"). f("app","le")=0 ("apple"). f("a","pp")=2 ("app", which both starts with "a" and ends with "pp").
5. How Should We Think?

Before scanning every word directly for each query (checking both startsWith and endsWith conditions one word at a time), notice that combining "suffix" and "word" into a SINGLE composite key at construction time reduces every future query to a single trie prefix search, answered efficiently regardless of dictionary size.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: A trie efficiently answers "does anything start with this exact prefix", but this problem needs BOTH a prefix and a suffix condition simultaneously.

Observation 2: For a given word, inserting the combo string (some suffix of the word) plus a separator character plus the FULL word, for EVERY possible suffix (from the whole word down to the empty suffix), covers every possible suffix that could ever be queried against this word.

Observation 3: A query f(prefix, suffix) becomes: does the string (suffix plus separator plus prefix) exist as a PREFIX of some inserted combo string? Walking the trie along this exact query string answers that directly.

Observation 4: Storing (and always overwriting with) the largest word index seen at every trie node visited during insertion means that by the time all words are inserted, every trie node already holds the largest index among all words passing through it, answering the "largest matching index" requirement without extra bookkeeping at query time.

This leads to inserting, for every word, every suffix-plus-separator-plus-word combo into one shared trie (tracking the max index at each node), then answering each query with a single trie walk along suffix-plus-separator-plus-prefix.
6. Brute Force Solution
For each query, scan every word directly, checking both the prefix and suffix conditions, tracking the largest matching index found.
Why the code is written this way

items: Checking both conditions directly against every word implements the definition simply.
This costs O(number of words times word length) per query, wasteful for up to 10^4 queries against up to 15000 words; a combined trie answers each query in one walk.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(number of words times word length) per query.
Space: O(total characters).
Limitation: combining suffix and word into one composite trie key, tracking the max index per node, reduces every future query to a single trie walk.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: At construction, for each word at index idx, for every possible suffix (from the full word down to the empty string), build the combo string as suffix plus a separator character (one guaranteed not to appear in any word, like "#") plus the full word. Insert this combo string into a trie, and at EVERY node passed through during insertion, overwrite that node's stored index with idx (words are processed in increasing index order, so later overwrites correctly keep the largest index). For a query f(prefix, suffix), build the search string as suffix plus the separator plus prefix, and walk the trie along it; if the walk succeeds, return the final node's stored index, otherwise return -1.
Insert every suffix-plus-separator-plus-word combo into one trie, storing the max index per node; answer each query with one trie walk along suffix-plus-separator-plus-prefix.
9. Optimized Solution
Dry run for words = ["apple"], query f("a","e")
Query f("a","e") builds the search string "e#a", which is a prefix of the inserted combo "e#apple", so the walk succeeds and returns index 0.
Why This Works

Every possible (suffix, prefix) pair a query could ask about a given word corresponds to exactly one of the suffix-plus-separator-plus-word combo strings inserted for that word, since every possible suffix of the word was covered during insertion. Because words are inserted in increasing index order and every visited node's stored index is unconditionally overwritten each time, by the end every node holds the LARGEST index among all words whose combo strings pass through it, so reading a node's stored index at query time directly yields the correct answer.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(total characters squared) for construction (each word contributes suffixes of total length up to word length squared), O(prefix length plus suffix length) per query.
Space: O(total characters squared) for the trie.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways
Prefix and Suffix Search is the classic "combine two conditions into one trie key using a separator" technique, additionally using overwrite-in-order to track the largest matching index.
Common Mistakes

items: Using a separator character that could actually appear inside a word, corrupting the combo key's uniqueness.
Forgetting to overwrite (not just conditionally update) the stored index at every visited node, which is what correctly captures "the largest index" given words are processed in order.

blocks.text: Edge Cases

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["No word matches both the prefix and suffix","Return -1."],["prefix or suffix is an empty string","An empty prefix or suffix matches trivially against any word for that respective condition."]]}

blocks.text: Interview Tips
Explicitly stating "combine both conditions into one search key with a separator, so one trie handles what would otherwise need two separate structures" demonstrates the core design insight clearly.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "match on both a prefix and a suffix simultaneously", think: combine them into one composite trie key using a separator character.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: How would this scale if word lengths were much larger, given the current approach's O(word length squared) construction cost per word?

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The direct-scan approach costs O(number of words times length) per query; the combined trie approach costs O(prefix length plus suffix length) per query, the standard efficient solution given the small word-length constraints here.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: combine two search conditions into one composite trie key using a separator character.
Core Idea: insert suffix plus separator plus full word for every suffix of every word, tracking the max index per node.
Time: O(number of words times length) per query for the brute force, O(prefix length plus suffix length) per query for the trie approach.
Space: O(total characters) for the brute force, O(total characters squared) for the trie approach.
Most Important Observation: a separator character lets one trie answer a two-condition query in a single walk.
Interview Difficulty: a clever trie-design problem combining multiple ideas.
One line memory trick: suffix, separator, word, all in one trie key.
